\begin{theorem}[Exponential bound for a linear-form tail moment]
\lean{FABL.expect_abs_linearForm_indicator_gt_le}
\proofsource{Analysis-of-Boolean-Functions-by-Ryan-ODonnell}{
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p128-b001,
  pdf-ffbe9c7b3306-p128-b002
}
\label{FABL.expect_abs_linearForm_indicator_gt_le}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.excess_abs_linearForm_expect_le, FABL.integral_uniformPMF_eq_expect, FABL.linearForm, FABL.uniformPMF, FABL.uniformRademacher_abs_linearForm_gt_le}
\difficulty{5}
Let $n$ be a nonnegative integer and let $a_1,\ldots,a_n$ be real coefficients
satisfying $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2=1$. For every real $s\geq1$, if $X$ is uniform on the
sign cube and $L(X)=\sum_{i=1}^n a_iX_i$, then
$\mathbb{E}\bigl[|L(X)|\,\mathbf{1}_{\{s<|L(X)|\}}\bigr]\leq(2s+2)\exp(-s^2/2)$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Expectation against a linear form]
\lean{FABL.expect_mul_levelOneLinearForm_eq}
\label{FABL.expect_mul_levelOneLinearForm_eq}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.linearForm, FABL.monomial}
\difficulty{3}
Let $n$ be a natural number, let $f$ be a real-valued function on the $n$-dimensional
sign cube, and let $a$ assign a real coefficient to each coordinate. The uniform
expectation of $f(x)$ times the linear form $\sum_{i=1}^n a_i x_i$ equals $\sum_{i=1}^n
a_i\widehat f(\{i\})$, where $\widehat f(\{i\})$ is the uniform expectation of
$f(x)x_i$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{theorem}[Vanishing Level-One Fourier Weight]
\lean{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eq_zero_of_zero_one_mean_eq_zero}
\label{FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eq_zero_of_zero_one_mean_eq_zero}
\leanok
\uses{FABL.fourierCoeff, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel, FABL.fourierWeightAtLevel_one_eq_sum_singleton, FABL.mean}
\difficulty{4}
Let $f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ take only the values $0$ and $1$, and suppose its
uniform mean on the Boolean cube is zero. Then its Fourier weight at level one is zero.
\end{theorem}

\difficulty{7}
There is a constant $C>0$ such that for every nonnegative integer $n$, every function
$f:\{-1,1\}^n\to\mathbb{R}$ taking only the values $0$ and $1$, and every real number
$\alpha$ satisfying $\mathbb{E}f=\alpha$ and $0<\alpha\le 1/2$, the level-one Fourier
weight of $f$ is at most $C\alpha^2\log_2(1/\alpha)$.
\end{theorem}
